blocks.text: Look into the wing mirror of a danfo bus and everything behind you appears small but you can see a wide sweep of the road. Look into the polished inside of a spoon and your face is upside down. Same light, same laws — the only thing that changed is the shape of the mirror.

blocks.title: The two laws of reflection
blocks.text: 1. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. 2. The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

blocks.caption: The second law of reflection, with both angles measured from the normal

blocks.markdown:
### Regular and diffuse reflection

A smooth, polished surface such as a silvered mirror sends a parallel beam out as a parallel beam. This is **regular** (specular) reflection, and it is what lets you see a clear image.

A rough surface such as a whitewashed wall or a page of this book scatters the beam in all directions. This is **diffuse** (irregular) reflection. No image forms, but the object becomes visible from every angle. Note carefully: the laws of reflection still hold at every single point of a rough surface — it is only because the normals point in different directions that the beam is scattered.

blocks.title: Two plane-mirror results worth memorising
blocks.text: If a plane mirror is rotated through an angle θ while the incident ray stays fixed, the reflected ray turns through 2θ. If two plane mirrors are inclined at an angle θ, the number of images formed is n = (360/θ) − 1.

blocks.title: A rotating mirror
blocks.prompt: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The mirror is then rotated through 12° about an axis in its own plane, while the incident ray is kept fixed. Through what angle does the reflected ray turn?

steps.text: Use the rotating-mirror result: the reflected ray turns through twice the angle turned by the mirror.
Substitute the rotation of the mirror.

blocks.caption: Image formation by a concave mirror. A convex mirror is much simpler: wherever the object is, the image is always virtual, erect and diminished.

blocks.markdown:
### The mirror formula

With the object distance $u$, the image distance $v$ and the focal length $f$ all measured from the pole:

$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v}$$

The **linear magnification** is

$$m = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{\text{image height}}{\text{object height}}$$

WAEC uses the **real-is-positive** convention: distances to real objects, real images and real foci are positive; distances to virtual images and to the virtual focus of a convex mirror are negative. So $f$ is **positive for a concave mirror** and **negative for a convex mirror**, and a negative $v$ in your answer means the image is virtual.

blocks.title: Concave mirror: finding the image distance
blocks.prompt: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.

steps.text: Write the mirror formula and make the unknown 1/v the subject.
Substitute f = +10 cm (concave, so positive) and u = 15 cm.
Invert to find v. It is positive, so the image is real.
The object lies between C (20 cm) and F (10 cm), which matches the table: the image is real, inverted, magnified and beyond C.

blocks.answer: A real, inverted image 30 cm in front of the mirror, twice the size of the object

blocks.title: Convex mirror: watch the sign of f
blocks.prompt: An object is placed 30 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.

steps.text: For a convex mirror the focus is virtual, so f is negative.
Substitute into the rearranged mirror formula.
Invert. The negative sign tells you the image is virtual, formed behind the mirror.
Find the magnification from the size of v.

blocks.answer: A virtual, erect image 10 cm behind the mirror, one-third the size of the object

blocks.title: Why mirrors are chosen the way they are
blocks.text: Convex mirrors are used as driving mirrors and in shops because they always give an erect image and cover a very wide field of view — the price paid is that everything looks smaller and therefore further away. Concave mirrors are used as shaving and dentists' mirrors (object closer than F gives a magnified erect image) and as reflectors in torches and car headlamps (a lamp at F sends out a parallel beam).

blocks.title: Three marks lost every year
blocks.text: Measure i and r from the NORMAL, not from the mirror surface — if a question says the ray makes 30° with the mirror, then i = 60°. Put f = −(value) for a convex mirror before you calculate. And remember that a virtual image can never be caught on a screen, no matter where you place the screen.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Work the mirror formula entirely in one unit — centimetres throughout, or metres throughout. Mixing them is the single commonest slip. If the question gives the radius of curvature, halve it first to get f.

points: The laws of reflection: incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
A plane mirror gives a virtual, erect, same-size, laterally inverted image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Rotating a plane mirror through θ turns the reflected ray through 2θ; two mirrors inclined at θ form (360/θ) − 1 images.
For a spherical mirror, r = 2f, and the mirror formula is 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with magnification m = v/u.
Using real-is-positive, f is positive for a concave mirror and negative for a convex mirror; a negative v means a virtual image.
A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image, which is why it is used as a driving mirror.
